description: Find the local LLM that actually runs and performs best on your hardware. Ranked by real, recency-aware benchmarks, not parameter count. One command, run it instantly.

detail.readme:
# whichllm [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/whichllm)](https://pypi.org/project/whichllm/) [![Python 3.11+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11+-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![Tests](https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Sponsor](https://img.shields.io/badge/Sponsor-GitHub%20Sponsors-EA4AAA?logo=githubsponsors)](https://github.com/sponsors/Andyyyy64)

**The smartest model your PC can actually run, including ones you didn't know it could.** whichllm reads your GPU, RAM and memory bandwidth, works out which open models fit and how fast each one will generate, and ranks them by benchmark results. Then it prints the command that runs the top pick the way it was estimated. [日本語版はこちら](docs/README.ja.md) ## Quick start ```bash uvx whichllm@latest ``` Shopping for a GPU? Simulate one: ```bash uvx whichllm@latest --gpu "RTX 4090" ``` To keep it around: ```bash uv tool install whichllm brew install andyyyy64/whichllm/whichllm pip install whichllm ``` ## Example A desktop with an 8 GB RTX 4060 and 32 GB of DDR4 (output trimmed): ```text $ whichllm # Model Quant Fit Speed Score 1 Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q6_K GPU+RAM 16 tok/s 68.8 2 unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-GGUF IQ4_XS Full GPU 37 tok/s 68.1 3 google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Q4_K_M GPU+RAM 11 tok/s 64.5 4 Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B Q5_K_M Full GPU 36 tok/s 64.2 5 zai-org/GLM-4.7-Flash Q5_K_M GPU+RAM 15 tok/s 62.3 #1 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also stands in for older generations of its line: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen_Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-GGUF Run #1 with llama.cpp: llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q6_K -c 4096 -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 35 -fa on ``` The top pick is a 35B model on an 8 GB card. It is a mixture-of-experts model, so each token only uses about 3B of its parameters. whichllm keeps attention, the shared weights and the KV cache in VRAM and leaves the experts of 35 of its 40 layers in system RAM, which is what llama.cpp's `--n-cpu-moe` does. The speed estimate counts only what each token reads from each place. A fits-in-VRAM check would have skipped the model, and treating it as a plain partial offload would have rated it far too slow. On a 24 GB RTX 4090 the same logic picks Qwen3.8-27B, although Qwen3-32B also fits there at Q4_K_M. The 27B is the newer generation of the same model line at about the same size and scores higher on current benchmarks, so the 32B is not listed separately; the note under the table names it. Speeds are estimates from memory bandwidth, not measurements of your machine. The table marks how confident each estimate is. Here is one checked on real hardware. On a 16 GB RTX 5080 with DDR5-5600, whichllm estimates 70 tok/s for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at Q4_K_M, with this command: ```bash llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q4_K_M -c 4096 -ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 15 -fa on ``` It measured 79 tok/s on llama.cpp b11977, from a 22 GB file on a 16 GB card. `whichllm bench` runs the same comparison on your machine. ## How it ranks Quality comes from Artificial Analysis and LiveBench, put on one scale and averaged. `--profile coding`, `math` and `vision` rank on benchmarks for that task instead, such as SciCode and LiveCodeBench for coding. The Open LLM Leaderboard and Chatbot Arena are frozen, so they only score models nothing current covers, and older generations are demoted. Each match records how it was found (the exact repo, its base model, a same-family interpolation, or the uploader's own claim) and weaker matches count for less. whichllm never recommends pretrain-only base checkpoints. To check the fit, memory is counted as weights plus a KV cache computed layer by layer from the model's `config.json` (grouped-query and latent attention, sliding windows, recurrent layers), plus runtime buffers. When a model does not fit in VRAM, a mixture-of-experts model first moves experts to RAM; any other model spills whole layers. Speed is bound by memory bandwidth: the GPU reads its share of the weights at VRAM speed and the CPU reads the rest at RAM speed. Both sides are calibrated against llama.cpp runs. Every placement is held to 8 tok/s: below that, a model's quality is scaled down, so a stronger model that would answer at 3 tok/s does not outrank one that answers at 25. The details are in [Scoring](docs/scoring.md) and [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md). ## How we test recommendations A wrong recommendation is a bug, so the rankings have regression tests: [`tests/golden/`](tests/golden/). - 29 hardware archetypes, from a 4 GB GTX 1650 to a 128 GB M4 Max and a DGX Spark, with AMD, Intel and mixed GPU sets, CPU-only boxes and 32K/128K-context setups, ranked against a frozen copy of the index: 1,430 models, most GGUF repos with their real file sizes. - 30 constraints describe what a good answer looks like instead of pinning an exact order: no pretrain-only checkpoints, draft heads or diffusion models, no outdated generation in the top 5, the top 3 stay within 1 tok/s of the 8 tok/s bar whenever the machine has that many options that fast, full-GPU rows keep their VRAM headroom and stay inside Metal's working set, `run` can launch the top rows, the newest dense 27B makes the top 3 on 24 GB+, a big MoE with experts in RAM makes the top 5 on a 16 GB card with 64 GB of RAM, and coding picks are not limited to models named "coder". - Speed and memory estimates stay within set bounds of real runs: an RTX 5080 and its CPU, plus 379 published llama.cpp results on 194 GPUs and 255 LocalScore results on 138 CPUs in [`tests/data/`](tests/data/). The estimator cannot drift without a test failing. - The top picks for every archetype are committed in [`top_picks.md`](tests/golden/top_picks.md), so any ranking change shows up as a diff in review. - A constraint that is known to fail is recorded with its reason as a strict expected failure. Fixing the bug turns it into a test failure until the record is removed. If whichllm picks something you would not run on your hardware, open an issue with the output. The 6 GB and RTX 3060 archetypes started as reports like that ([#76](https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm/issues/76), [#104](https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm/issues/104)). ## Commands ```bash whichllm # best models for this machine whichllm --gpu "RTX 5060 Ti" # simulate a GPU (add --vram 16 for a variant) whichllm --gpu "2x RTX 3090" # or several whichllm --profile coding # general, coding, vision, math, any whichllm --context-length 64k # long context changes what fits whichllm --gpu-only # only models that fit entirely in VRAM whichllm --speed usable # hide anything under 8 tok/s whichllm --markdown # pasteable table for issues and chats whichllm --json # rows include placement and the run recipe whichllm hardware # what was detected whichllm engines # which inference engines run here whichllm plan "qwen3 32b" # what GPU a model needs whichllm upgrade "RTX 4090" "RTX 5090" # compare against candidate GPUs whichllm run # download the top pick and chat with it whichllm bench # measure the top pick on this machine whichllm report # share that measurement in a GitHub issue whichllm snippet # print Python that loads the top pick ``` Every option is in the [CLI reference](docs/cli.md). If LM Studio complains that a pick is slightly too large, ask for a more conservative fit: ```bash whichllm --gpu-only --speed usable --vram-headroom 1.5GB ``` If an integrated GPU or unified memory is detected with the wrong limits, override them with `--vram` and `--ram-bandwidth` (see [Hardware](docs/hardware.md)). ## Run and snippet `whichllm run` downloads the model and opens a chat. Without a model name it takes the top pick. ![run demo](assets/demo-run.gif) ```bash whichllm run whichllm run "qwen 2.5 1.5b gguf" whichllm run "phi 3 mini gguf" --cpu-only ``` With llama.cpp installed (`brew install llama.cpp`, `winget install ggml.llamacpp`), a GGUF model runs in its `llama-cli` with the flags of the printed recipe, so the chat uses the GPU and keeps MoE experts in RAM the way the ranking estimated. A named model is left to llama.cpp's automatic fit. A GGUF model already installed in LM Studio is opened from that library instead of being downloaded again; `whichllm recommend` marks those rows `Installed`. Pass `--lm-studio-path` (repeatable) for a legacy or custom library: ```bash whichllm run "qwen 2.5 1.5b gguf" --lm-studio-path /mnt/models/lm-studio ``` Without llama-cli, `run` creates a throwaway environment with `uv` and uses `llama-cpp-python` for GGUF models and `transformers` for the rest. PyPI only ships llama-cpp-python as source, so the first run compiles it, which took 22 minutes on a Core Ultra 9, and that build runs on the CPU only. See [Run and snippet](docs/run-snippet.md). ## Where the data comes from whichllm reads a prebuilt index: the Hugging Face model list, each family's `config.json` and the merged benchmark scores, rebuilt daily on GitHub Actions and published only if it passes quality checks. A cold start takes about a second and makes no Hugging Face API calls. `--live` fetches everything directly instead, and `HF_TOKEN` is used when set. ## Documentation - [CLI reference](docs/cli.md) - [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md) - [Scoring](docs/scoring.md) - [Hardware detection and simulation](docs/hardware.md) - [Run and snippet](docs/run-snippet.md) - [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) ## Development ```bash git clone https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm.git cd whichllm uv sync --locked --dev uv run whichllm uv run pytest ``` Ranking changes need a look at the golden snapshot: `uv run python scripts/update_golden.py report`. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Support If whichllm saved you a bad download or a bad hardware purchase, sponsoring helps keep it maintained: hardware reports, benchmark updates, packaging and support for more machines. It stays open source either way. A star helps other people find it. I'd also like to hear what it picked for your machine, so feel free to drop it in [Issues](https://github.com/Andyyyy64/whichllm/issues). ## Star History [![Star History Chart](https://star-history.dera.page/svg?repos=Andyyyy64/whichllm&type=Date)](https://star-history.dera.page/#Andyyyy64/whichllm&Date) ## License MIT
